papers.title: Astrocytic timekeepers and their influence on brain waste clearance in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.summary: This paper discusses how astrocytes, a type of brain support cell, contain internal circadian clock mechanisms that regulate daily rhythms of brain activity. These 'astrocytic timekeepers' appear to influence the brain's waste clearance systems, such as the glymphatic pathway, which removes toxic proteins during sleep. The paper connects disruptions in this circadian-astrocyte-clearance axis to the buildup of pathological proteins seen in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.why: Although focused on astrocytes rather than neurons, this work is relevant because impaired waste clearance and circadian dysregulation intersect with autophagy/mitophagy pathways that maintain neuronal proteostasis, which could inform how perineuronal net and interneuron health are affected by failed clearance mechanisms in neurodegeneration.
papers.figure: A schematic figure illustrating the circadian regulation of astrocytic function and its coupling to glymphatic/waste clearance flow across the sleep-wake cycle.

papers.title: miR-378f targets CAB39 to regulate autophagy in chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy.
papers.summary: This study investigates how miR-378f, a small regulatory RNA, controls the protein CAB39 to influence autophagy processes. The research focuses on chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, a condition where nerve damage occurs as a side effect of cancer treatment. By showing that this microRNA-CAB39 pathway regulates autophagy, the authors suggest a potential mechanism and therapeutic target for this painful neuropathy.
papers.why: While this paper centers on peripheral nerves rather than brain interneurons, it offers mechanistic insight into autophagy regulation in neuronal damage that could inform parallel investigations of mitophagy pathways in central nervous system neurons.
papers.figure: A figure showing autophagy markers (e.g., LC3, p62) and CAB39 expression levels in neurons with and without miR-378f manipulation, ideally correlated with neuropathy severity or morphological changes.

papers.title: Epigallocatechin Gallate-Primed Bone Marrow Mesenchymal Stem Cell-Derived Extracellular Vesicles Attenuate Endothelial Senescence by Modulating PI3K/AKT/mTOR Signaling and PINK1-Associated Mitochondrial Quality Control.
papers.summary: This study shows that extracellular vesicles secreted by bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, when pretreated with epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG, a green tea compound), can reduce signs of aging in endothelial cells. The protective effect works by adjusting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, which controls cell growth and stress responses. It also involves PINK1-related mitochondrial quality control, a process that identifies and removes damaged mitochondria to keep cells healthy.
papers.why: Although focused on endothelial cells rather than neurons, this paper's mechanistic insights into PINK1-associated mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control pathways are directly relevant background for understanding analogous mitophagy processes being studied in neurons and interneurons.
papers.figure: A figure showing PINK1/Parkin-related mitophagy markers and mitochondrial morphology/quality metrics in EGCG-EV-treated versus untreated senescent endothelial cells.

papers.title: CCR5, CD163, CSF1R, and FCGR3A as Candidate Biomarkers Associated With Mitophagy in Atherosclerosis.
papers.summary: This study investigates four genes—CCR5, CD163, CSF1R, and FCGR3A—as potential biomarkers linked to mitophagy (the process of clearing damaged mitochondria) in atherosclerosis, a disease involving plaque buildup in arteries. Using bioinformatics approaches, likely including gene expression analysis and immune cell profiling, the researchers identify these genes as candidates for diagnosing or understanding mitophagy-related processes in vascular disease. The findings suggest these markers may help explain how mitochondrial quality control relates to immune cell activity in atherosclerotic plaques.
papers.why: While focused on cardiovascular disease rather than brain tissue, this paper offers transferable insight into mitophagy biomarker discovery methodology that could inform analogous searches for mitophagy markers in neuronal or glial populations.

papers.title: CDKN1B undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation and attenuates lipid accumulation and inflammatory response by promoting mitophagy in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
papers.summary: This study reports that the protein CDKN1B can undergo liquid-liquid phase separation, a process where proteins form droplet-like condensates inside cells. In the context of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, this phase separation behavior of CDKN1B helps promote mitophagy (selective clearance of damaged mitochondria), which in turn reduces fat buildup and inflammation in liver cells. The findings suggest a new molecular mechanism linking protein condensate formation to mitochondrial quality control and metabolic disease.
papers.why: Although this paper is about liver disease rather than brain tissue, it offers mechanistic insight into how phase separation can regulate mitophagy, a core process central to this PhD project on neuronal mitophagy and autophagy.
papers.figure: A figure showing CDKN1B condensate formation alongside mitophagy markers (e.g., colocalization of CDKN1B droplets with mitochondrial/autophagosome markers) would be most informative.

papers.title: RIPK3 Promotes Gingival Fibroblast Apoptosis and Periodontal Inflammatory Injury by Impairing Mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study looks at periodontal (gum) disease and finds that a protein called RIPK3 drives gum fibroblast cells to die via apoptosis. The mechanism involves RIPK3 blocking mitophagy, the process that clears out damaged mitochondria. When mitophagy is impaired, mitochondrial damage accumulates, worsening inflammation and tissue injury in the gums.
papers.why: Although this paper is about gum tissue rather than brain or neurons, it offers a mechanistic parallel for how RIPK3-mediated inhibition of mitophagy drives cell death and inflammatory injury, a pathway relevant to neuronal mitophagy dysfunction.

papers.title: Ginsenoside Rg1 promotes mitophagy and delays aging through the DAF-16 in Caenorhabditis elegans.
papers.summary: This study investigates ginsenoside Rg1, a compound from ginseng, and its effects on aging in the roundworm C. elegans. The researchers found that Rg1 promotes mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, and extends lifespan. These effects appear to depend on the DAF-16 transcription factor, a key regulator of stress resistance and longevity pathways.
papers.why: Although this is a worm study rather than neuronal/brain tissue, it offers mechanistic insight into mitophagy regulation and longevity pathways that could inform hypotheses about mitochondrial quality control in aging neurons relevant to the PhD project.

papers.title: Saikosaponin A promotes diabetic wound healing by suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome-associated macrophage pyroptosis and modulating mitophagy-related signaling.
papers.summary: This study looks at Saikosaponin A, a plant-derived compound, and its effect on healing diabetic wounds. The researchers found it works by blocking a cell death process called pyroptosis in macrophages, which is driven by the NLRP3 inflammasome. It also appears to influence mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, as part of its healing mechanism.
papers.why: Although focused on diabetic wounds and macrophages rather than neurons, the paper's mechanistic focus on mitophagy-related signaling as a therapeutic lever could offer transferable insights into mitophagy regulation relevant to the neuronal context of this PhD project.
